theme: The altar of incense, anointing oil, bronze basin, the Sabbath
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 30:1-31:18. Today’s reading finishes the instructions for the tabernacle with several smaller items and ends with a reminder about the Sabbath. Watch for the repeated theme of consecration, and notice how the Sabbath fits into the story.
settingTheScene: God has described the ark, the table, the lampstand, the tent, the altar, and the priests. Chapter 30 adds a few more items: the altar of incense, a half-shekel census tax for atonement, the bronze basin for washing, the anointing oil, and the incense. Chapter 31 names the craftsmen, Bezalel and Oholiab, who are filled with God’s Spirit to do the work. It closes with the Sabbath command and with God giving Moses the two tablets. The next chapter will show how fast things can go wrong.
observation: The altar of incense stands before the veil, and incense is burned on it every morning and evening (30:1-10).
Each person aged twenty and over pays a half shekel as a ransom for his life, “that there be no plague among them” (30:11-16). The rich do not pay more and the poor do not pay less.
Aaron and his sons must wash their hands and feet at the bronze basin “so that they may not die” (30:17-21).
The anointing oil is a special recipe, and it is not to be used for ordinary purposes (30:22-33).
The incense is “holy,” and no one may make it for himself (30:34-38).
Bezalel is “filled with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship” (31:1-5).
The Sabbath is a sign between God and Israel “throughout your generations, that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you” (31:13).
“He gave to Moses, when he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone, written with the finger of God” (31:18).
interpretation:
Several themes run through these chapters. The first is atonement. The half-shekel ransom is the first time the word appears in the context of money. Everyone pays the same, because every life is equally in need of covering. No one can say that he is better than his neighbor, and no one can say that he is too poor to be included. The ransom is a quiet equalizer.

The second is the pattern of washing before service. The priests have to wash their hands and feet “so that they may not die.” The language is stark. God’s holiness is not something to take lightly. The bronze basin is placed between the altar and the tent, so a priest passes it on the way in. The point is cleanliness. A sinner does not approach a holy God casually.

The third is the Spirit-filled craftsman. It is a remarkable detail. Bezalel is the first person in the Bible described as filled with the Spirit of God, and the gift is for craftsmanship: woodworking, metalwork, and cutting stones. The Spirit is not only for prophets and priests. He equips people for skilled work in the service of God. If you have a skill, whether in teaching, building, cooking, or counting, it is a gift from the Spirit of God.

The fourth is the Sabbath. After all the instructions for building a sanctuary, God ends with the Sabbath. It is a deliberate order. The people are about to build a holy place, and God reminds them that holiness is also a matter of time. The Sabbath is a sign of the covenant, a reminder that Israel does not hold itself together by work. God is the one who sanctifies them. Even the project of building the tabernacle has to stop on the seventh day.

The final verse looks ahead. God writes on the tablets with his own finger. Moses will come down in the next chapter to a camp that has already broken the covenant.
connection: Paul says that believers are not our own: we were “bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:20). Peter says it was “not with perishable things such as silver or gold” but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18-19). The Spirit who filled Bezalel fills every believer (Acts 2:4; Ephesians 1:13), and Paul lists the gifts he gives for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:4-11). Hebrews 4:9-10 says that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God.
application:
Thank God that the price of your redemption is the same for everyone, and that you cannot buy your way into his favor.

Think of the abilities God has given you. Ask the Spirit to help you use one of them this week in service to his people.

Treat the Sabbath as a gift. Ask yourself whether you are truly resting on the one day in seven set apart for it.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that you are not your own.
Ask him to fill you with his Spirit and use your skills for his glory.
Ask him to teach you to rest in him.
